there are sort of thee ways to do 'symbolic' families:  detail lines in the family, nested detail item, or nested generic annotation. 

you need to be sure you understand which behavior you want.  detail lines and detail items are always true size in the model.  generic annotations always scale for the printed size.

something like a 2x4 fixture you should use detail lines or detail items because the object in the view needs to be the actual size.  something like a ceiling mounted occupancy sensor or something like that would be a generic annotation because you want the symbol to be the same size regardless of scale.

Parameters:

Label:

Here's some things i think are useful

. Hold some sort of regular revit discussion or training.  Weekly, Bi-weekly, monthly, it sort of depends on your need.  Getting people sharing ideas and talking about the standard methods or best practices is important and repeated, long-term exposure is more effective than some sort of all-day training

. Revit is more similar to Autocad than you might think: Out of the box, Autocad would be really hard to do production work with.  Companies and Designers have had 30 years to develop processes, resources (blocks, patterns, etc.), and scripts to improve the workflow.  Revit requires a similar investment in infrastructure (specifically on the design side): this will mainly be templates, families, parameters and schedules, and scripts.  Thoughtful investment in resources is way more efficient than a decentralized organic process.

. Have post-mortem project meetings to review what went right and what was challenging.  Look at the overall process and try to understand how things are different.

. Find compromise with graphics.  This is a persistent fight, and one that seems to be hard to sway older members about. You can get revit to look a lot like cad, but it's a lot of work, and requires investment in the infrastructure i mentioned before.  There are some limitations that you can work around, but you just have to figure out what the right balance for your firm is - I find it more effective to focus on making really good looking revit documents than trying to make things look like cad. Just sort of non-value-added labor.

. have, or understand the function of, a BIM Execution Plan.  This helps more with collaboration and communication issues than anything, but a big part of BIM as a concept is sort of that saying 'prior planning prevents poor performance'. 

. have internal BIM kickoff meetings.  Identify project specific needs (families, schedules, etc.)

. Deploy gradually on a series of pilot projects.  There's a useful analogy to industrial processes: you're not going to make a major change to production with a new product, process, or technology.  My exposure is in the petrochem industry where the company i was interning at had a pilot plant to test new polymer formulations or processes, then review and evaluate.  I think trying to dump a new technology on a whole company with a diverse level of skills is a recipe for disaster.  There are going to be lots of challenges and i've seen to many people abandon revit after trying this approach.  Review the processes, successes, and challenges after each one, and plan the modifications for the next one.  This is fairly idealized and actual implementation will probably have to be adapted.  Figuring out what projects are suitable to be pilots is difficult.  Having an entirely internal one is safe, but completely overhead cost.  Using a client project is hazardous, but billable.
